analysis.one_liner: Requires large multinational companies to publicly report profits and taxes country by country.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2026 with one cosponsor and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, where it has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require large multinational companies that file with the Securities and Exchange Commission to publish, in a public online database, how much revenue and profit they book in each country and how much tax they actually pay there. It covers every subsidiary a company owns, including those registered in tax havens and in U.S. territories with their own tax systems. The goal is to make it visible when a company reports most of its profits in a low-tax country while doing most of its business elsewhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers and small businesses get a clearer picture of which multinational corporations shift profits into low-tax jurisdictions, which has historically reduced the tax base that funds public services. Investors, journalists, and regulators also gain machine-readable data to compare what companies say publicly with what they report for tax purposes.

how_it_helps.text: Each covered company would have to file a report listing every subsidiary, where it is resident for tax purposes, its revenues, profit before tax, income tax paid, employees, and assets, broken down by tax jurisdiction [S2].
The reports must be submitted in a machine-readable format and made available to the public online, so anyone — not just regulators — can search the data [S2].

The bill applies to companies that are members of multinational groups with annual revenue above a threshold set by the SEC to conform to U.S. or international country-by-country reporting standards, so it targets the largest global firms [S2].
The SEC must issue a proposed rule within 270 days and a final rule within one year of enactment, with reporting taking effect one year after the final rule [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large multinational corporations bear the compliance cost of assembling and filing the country-by-country data, and they lose a degree of financial privacy that currently allows profits to be booked in low-tax jurisdictions without public scrutiny.

drawbacks.text: Multinational companies would face real compliance costs to collect, standardize, and file detailed financial data for every subsidiary and jurisdiction, and foreign competitors not listed on U.S. exchanges would not face the same requirement [S2].

Disclosure alone does not change any tax rates or close any loopholes; the bill only makes information public, so its practical effect depends on how regulators, tax authorities, and investors use the data [S2].
The revenue threshold for which companies are covered is left to the SEC rather than fixed in the bill, which adds uncertainty for businesses and could delay or narrow implementation [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit — visibility into where the world's largest companies book profits and pay taxes — is broad and cheap to deliver, since the data largely already exists for tax authorities under international country-by-country reporting standards. The main costs fall on the multinationals themselves as compliance expenses and on companies whose tax arrangements would become publicly awkward. The honest limitation is that this is a transparency bill, not a tax-collection bill: it exposes profit shifting but does not directly stop it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or floor action, and the current session ends in early January 2027.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on July 16, 2026, by Rep. Brittany Pettersen, joined by one cosponsor, and referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1] [S2].
The complete action history shows only two steps: introduction and committee referral, with no markup, hearing, or vote recorded since [S4].
Congress is still in session until January 3, 2027, but a bill introduced in mid-July of the second session with one cosponsor has not moved in committee [S1] [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large multinational corporations and jurisdictions that host offshore entities are better off for now, since the disclosure requirement exists only on paper and no committee or floor action has been scheduled that could make it law.

for.name: Rep. Brittany Pettersen
for.role: Sponsor, introduced the bill and referred it to committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Disclosure of Tax Havens and Offshoring Act on July 16, 2026

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor are Democrats, but no Republican or industry group has taken a recorded position on the bill, and no vote has occurred.

industries.note: They would have to publish, country by country, where they book profits and pay taxes, exposing arrangements that shift taxable profit into low-tax jurisdictions. That visibility costs them privacy and reputational leverage, while the public gains information it has never had.

industries.industry: Tax-haven financial services and jurisdictions with fiscal autonomy
industries.note: Their business depends on hosting subsidiaries whose local profits and taxes stay out of public view; mandatory disclosure makes those arrangements visible in a public database. The bill's definition explicitly includes non-country jurisdictions with fiscal autonomy and U.S. territories with their own tax systems [S2].
The SEC gains a new disclosure regime to write rules for and enforce within a year of enactment, adding workload but strengthening its dataset on listed multinationals.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has one cosponsor, was introduced in the second half of the session, and has had no committee action. Bills at this stage in a new committee rarely reach a markup or floor vote before the Congress ends, so the most likely path is that it expires in committee unless the sponsor builds cosponsor support quickly; it could be reintroduced in the next Congress.
